title: I Ate 100 Pounds of Meat in 30 Days — Here's Why
description: I ate over 100 pounds of meat in 30 days. And that’s not the craziest part. But before I tell you what happened we need context. The carnivore diet has had a fascinating trajectory over the past decade. It exploded into the mainstream as prominent advocates promoted it as a solution for everything from improving athletic performance and body composition to treating obesity, autoimmune disease, and other chronic illnesses. Recently, though, the narrative seems to have shifted. To many people, it looks like carnivore is on the decline. Part of that perception comes from some of its biggest public advocates moving away from strict carnivore. Perhaps the most notable example is Dr. Paul Saladino—better known as the Carnivore MD —who reintroduced fruit and other plant foods. So... did the carnivore diet fail? Did it simply follow the predictable life cycle of every fad diet? Is it fading away like a cauliflower fart in the wind? Not exactly. Because beneath the internet debates and social media hot takes is a much more nuanced story. And that’s what made me want to revisit the topic and re-try carnivore for myself. In fact, this wasn’t my first experience with carnivore. A few years ago, I followed the diet for five months, and overall, I had a surprisingly positive experience. Although, to be fair, my prior version was fairly liberal. I ate dairy, eggs, and... if I’m being honest... I also cheated with coffee. (Although I suppose if it had been kopi luwak, you could argue it was technically animal-based.) This time, though, I wanted to go further. More extreme. So, I went whole hog. Or perhaps, more appropriately... all cow. For 30 days, I followed the Lion Diet —the strictest version of carnivore. No dairy. No eggs. No seafood.

title: Are You An Exercise Non-Responder?
description: Do you get the feeling that your workouts just aren’t working? You show up day after day, week after week, month after month. You put in the work. And yet, the results don’t match the effort. You start to wonder: Shouldn’t I be seeing more gains for my effort? Am I just unlucky? It feels almost conspiratorial to say out loud. And nobody wants to be a whiner. So, you keep going, and you keep quiet. But that phenomenon is real. It’s been recognized for years. In fact, the fitness world even has a name for it: “ non-responders ” or “ low-responders ” to exercise. The implication is that some unlucky people just don’t respond as well. And it’s usually chalked up to bad genetics. The good news is that when you actually dig into the data, the story is far more nuanced, and far more actionable! Today, we’re delving into a study that cracks open the mystery of exercise “non-responsiveness.” And the answer isn’t genetics. It’s something else entirely that is completely within your control. Premium subscribers get full access to my deep dives into cutting-edge metabolic research for less than $1/letter, 3 per week. You’ll always walk away with at least one new insight about metabolic health. In the rest of this letter for StayCurious Metabolism Premium members, we dive into: The real culprit behind exercise non-responsiveness A combination of animal and human data Actionable strategies you can use today to get more out of every workout. If you want to join a community of people who care deeply about metabolic health, and who aren’t satisfied with surface-level answers, now is as good a time as any! title: Lp(a) Masterclass: What It Is and What to Do About It
description: *News note: The big news of the last few days was the negative result of the Lp(a) HORIZON trial, a large Phase 3 trial in which an Lp(a)-lowering drug failed to reduce cardiovascular events. The cardiology world is in a little bit of a free fall right now. Whether or not you’re aware of this trial, I’ll provide my commentary in a postscript at the end. All the teachings herein still apply. You just get a little extra nuance. When I was first diagnosed with elevated Lp(a), I was scared. I knew what the numbers meant. Statistically, my lifetime risk of a heart attack was dramatically higher—perhaps by as much as 230% . And because heart disease runs in my family, this wasn’t just an abstract statistic. I inherited high Lp(a) from my father, who almost died of a heart attack at just 44 years old. I had every reason to be frightened. I’m not anymore. What changed wasn’t my genetics. My Lp(a) is still high. What changed was my understanding. The Lp(a) Myth Over the past few years, Lp(a) has gone from obscurity to becoming the newest cardiovascular supervillain. Darth Vader. Thanos. Voldemort. Pick your franchise. And if you’re interested in heart health, you’ve almost certainly heard that elevated Lp(a) substantially increases cardiovascular risk. What you may also have heard is that “ it’s almost entirely genetic .” And “ there are no medications available shown to lower Lp(a) and reduce cardiovascular risk .” Those statements have truth to them. There’s also, “ so there’s nothing you can do about it .” That one? That one is dead wrong. While your Lp(a) level is largely determined by your genes, the amount Lp(a) increases your cardiovascular risk is not. Point blank.
